profile: Opens a paragraph on the last one's point, often as a conditional or a restated premise: 'If the signs are present and plain and yet we still pass them by, the fault is on our side.' / 'Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences.'
Ends a paragraph on the point itself, sometimes with a short concrete line rather than an aphorism: 'Most of us see only the lamp.'
Often ends a paragraph with a plain forward link into a verse: 'The Qur'an describes the gap in one verse.'
Explains every quotation after giving it, in plain terms: 'Cattle see and hear perfectly well, so the comparison cannot be about the senses.'

Sentences are mid-length and plain. 'And' joins two clauses at most. Semicolons and 'whereas' are used for contrast: 'God is not withholding signs; we are failing to receive them.' / 'Eyes and ears take in the surface of things, whereas inside a human being...'
Brings in sources by full name with a light verb, then moves on: 'Mohammad Ali Shomali makes the same point, describing...'; 'ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi explains what passing by a sign means'
Uses 'he says' as a parenthetical, but sparingly, about once a paragraph: 'Most pious people, he says, even those careful about the shariʿa...'
Uses an inclusive 'we' and 'let's' to walk alongside the reader, never to scold: 'Let's start with two claims.'; 'We have heard these verses many times'
Written register with concrete images (red lamp, rusted machine). Diction is plain, with few abstractions.
Numbers and structures the argument explicitly: 'The first is...', 'The second claim goes further'
Never uses rhetorical questions, jokes, dramatic fragments or suspense. Never restates a conclusion it has just drawn.

tells: Opens on the last point ('takes this humility further') and explains the Munajat line straight after quoting it ('even the turning towards God is His doing'); plain, linked paragraphs.

The ordinal structure ('The second gift', 'The third gift') and the bridging question-free link 'None of this would matter... Surah al-Nisaʾ answers that concern' match A; slightly loose line on the muqarrabun after the Yunus verse.

'Purification, in his account, is polishing the soul so that it starts working' — restates the paragraph's own first sentence ('polish the soul by doing whatever the Prophet has asked'); Author A would move straight on to the Chapter One link
'the Sheikh adds... the Sheikh says... the Sheikh says' — attribution used as filler in every paragraph; Author A names the source once and then explains

'The sentence divides the work. Purification is the traveller's part; the light is Allah's to give.' — tidy closing antithesis that adds nothing to the quotation it follows; Author A's paragraph endings land on a concrete point

'The two words are kept apart here only as a working distinction... He separates the words to make the difference between the two kinds of knowing easier to see.' — a whole paragraph making a true side remark and then saying it again; it does not move the argument on, which Author A's paragraphs always do
'A person does not try to understand their hunger; they arrive at it and feel it.' — a neat aphoristic gloss; Author A explains with an example rather than with a maxim

'The severance the prayers ask for is therefore in the heart, not in the household or the marketplace.' then 'What the prayer asks to lose is the heart's love for the world, not the world itself or the people and the work in it.' — the same conclusion restated across paragraphs; Author A states it once

'He places this severance a step beyond... that Chapter One described' followed at once by 'It is the severance Chapter One found in the friends of God' — two back-references in a row; Author A links once and then moves forward

The numbered requests and the explanation after each quotation ('In this request the heart is brought near by its own passion for God') match Author A; 'read several of its lines to his listeners' is slightly looser than usual.

The chapter opening mirrors the reference ('These words come from...'); 'Let's start with the order' matches 'Let's start with two claims'; the link back to the previous chapter is explicit and plain.

The source is named once with a light verb, then the passage explains why it is cited ('He cites them to show...'); after the quotation it explains ('The servant stands there because of need...'); the transition 'as a pupil would' picks up the previous paragraph.
'Then: "These are shirk."' — a dramatic spoken fragment; Author A would write a full sentence such as 'He then called them shirk'

'The great teachers of the Shia tradition make closely related points, each in his own words.' — opens a catalogue of three teachers making the same point, each paragraph adding a true remark without moving the argument; Author A cites one confirming source and moves on
'Shirk, setting up a partner beside God, is the gravest charge in Islam.' — an emphatic closing line for effect; Author A ends on the argument's point

Concrete explanation (hadd also means a limit; 'the rational animal' drawing a line round us); paragraphs open on the previous point ('The second kind...', 'Knowledge by presence is complete...'). The anxiety coda is slightly extra.

'Having done this, the traveller waits for Allah's help and looks to nothing else... That life comes, he says, when a person follows the Prophet completely and then waits for the help of Allah.' — the same point said twice in one paragraph; Author A says it once

'Three of the great teachers of the tradition speak to how fikr and suluk relate. For Imam Khomeini and ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi...' — announces three and names two, a looser setup than Author A's exact enumerations

'He adds that... The sciences, he goes on, are... In another place he gives the view...' — attribution stacked as filler, with quotations ('tear it into shreds') left unexplained; Author A explains each quotation

'If the faculty can be repaired, there should be people in whom it already works' picks up the last point in A's conditional style; each verse gets a plain explanation ('A heart trembles only at the mention of someone it has some experience of').

'ordinary people, he says,... It is difficult, he says,... yet he says... A human being, he says' — 'he says' four times in one paragraph as filler; Author A uses it once and then speaks in its own voice
'This is the case for pursuing ʿirfan. The Qur'an invites more than the minimum...' — a paragraph that restates the chapter's conclusion; Author A does not summarise what it has just argued
'Pursuing ʿirfan means training the soul and soul-training is not unique to Islam.' — opens a new subject rather than picking up the previous paragraph, joined by a loose 'and'

Opens on the previous verse ('The people of this verse fear Him...'), explains the quotation from Imam ʿAli in plain terms, and uses ordinal structure ('The first gift is nearness') with a concrete gloss on muqarrabun.

The opening picks up the previous point; the passage explains the hadith afterwards ('The hadith sets the two kinds of knowing side by side'); it closes on a plain forward link into the Surah al-Nur verse, as Author A does.
